title: Kernel Bridge Experiments: async eviction + KVCache scheduling notes
content:
Purpose / scope:
This doc captures our exploratory experiments and decision notes for an intermediate "kernel bridge" layer that unifies execution across TensorRT, Triton, and small custom CUDA kernels. Focus areas: async kernel invocation, KV cache memory management and eviction, scheduling heuristics for mixed-batch workloads, and failure/fallback tradeoffs. Goal is to drive an implementable design for Q4 that minimizes tail-latency regressions while keeping peak throughput on par with native integrations.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- A kernel-bridge abstraction that exposes async enqueue/complete semantics and a light-weight queue per-GPU allows efficient co-scheduling of TRT engines, Triton model instances, and our small custom ops.
- KV cache eviction should be prioritized by predicted reuse (time-decay score) and model locality; background async eviction (non-blocking) reduces p99 impact but increases memory churn and requires robust backpressure.
- Triton gives best multi-model management and easy scaling, TensorRT wins for single-model dense throughput (especially INT8/FP16), custom kernels are essential for sparsity/attention optimizations. The bridge must therefore allow per-request routing and dynamic fallback.
- Immediate risks: increased complexity in resource accounting, harder debugging when cross-framework failures occur, and the need for tighter CI for correctness across all three stacks.

Experiment notes (setup):
- Hardware: 4x A100-80GB and 2x H100-80GB nodes.
- Workloads: conversational workloads with sequence lengths 64/128/512, mix: 70% short (64), 25% medium (128), 5% long (512). Also a bursty embedding path (batchable).
- Models: LLaMA-2-13B as our primary load (TRT engine + FP16 & int8 calib), and a smaller 3B used as a fall-back Triton instance.
- Key metrics: token latency p50/p95/p99, tokens/s throughput, memory high-water mark, cpu/gpu utilization, KVCache hit ratio, number of context evictions per minute.

Findings (quantified):
- Baseline: Triton-only deployment (one instance per-GPU pinned) -> steady throughput ~18k tokens/s per A100 for 13B FP16, p99 ~230ms for short sequences.
- TRT engine (native TRT inference) -> +22% throughput for steady-state, but spikes in p99 when small batches and async submission collide; we saw p99 up to 420ms when host enqueue blocked due to kernel launch contention.
- Custom kernels used for fused attention (sparse) reduced tokens/s variance and improved mean latency by ~8% on long sequences but required separate memory pools for workspace sizing.
- Combined bridge: allowing requests to be routed to TRT engine when model pinned and to Triton fallback when memory pressure high gave us best-of-both: ~15% throughput gain over Triton-only and p99 within 1.1x of Triton baseline in most traffic patterns.

Design proposals and tradeoffs:
1) Async enqueue + completion queue (kernel-bridge API)
   - API surface: enqueue_async(request_id, engine_handle, input_ptrs, callback_id) and poll_completion(timeout_ms).
   - Tradeoff: less blocking means higher concurrency but exposes us to more complex ordering and host-side queue bloat. We observed a pathological case where input buffers queued faster than GPU could free KV cache entries, leading to memory spikes.
   - Mitigation: integrate backpressure tokens with our router; when host-queue length > threshold, start redirecting new requests to lower-fidelity model variants or reject with 503 throttling.

2) KV cache eviction strategies
   - Options we tried: LRU, time-decay (exponential), predicted-reuse (ML heuristic trained on session traces).
   - LRU: simple but evicts long-tail-of-active sessions that have occasional long pauses -> caused re-population penalties (cold-start token spikes).
   - Time-decay: better for conversation traffic, maintains hot sessions; p99 improved by ~18% vs LRU in mixed workloads.
   - Predicted-reuse (offline model): best theoretical performance but expensive to maintain and brittle on distribution shift.
   - Proposal: default to time-decay with per-session weights; expose hooks for admins to pin sessions (prevent eviction) and implement an optional predicted-reuse service as an opt-in feature for Dedicated customers.

3) Scheduling heuristics for mixed-batch workloads
   - Observed modes: (a) many small low-latency requests, (b) large batched throughput jobs (embeddings/sync-generation), (c) long sequence continuation requests with high KVCache locality.
   - Heuristic: maintain three logical queues per-GPU (latency-queue, batch-queue, continuation-queue). Priority: latency > continuation > batch but allow small preemption windows for batch jobs to avoid starvation.
   - Implementation detail: use a preemption token system where batch kernels are scheduled in 8-16ms slices and can be evicted mid-run only if a higher-priority request arrives and the kernel supports checkpoint/resume (requires kernel support). For kernels that cannot be preempted (many TRT engines), we instead reserve a small capacity for latency queue to avoid full blocking.

4) Memory pools and workspace management
   - TRT engines often expose opaque workspace requirements. We maintain two GPU memory pools: one for KV cache (large, long-lived), and one for transient workspace (small, short-lived).
   - Transient allocator must be fast and support asynchronous free (free after CUDA event). We used per-stream ring allocators with epoch-based reclamation.
   - For long-lived allocations we use a soft quota and an eviction watermark (trigger time-decay eviction at 75% occupancy).

5) Fallback and graceful degradation policies
   - When per-GPU memory > 85% or enqueue queue > N, we trigger fallback steps in order: (1) route to smaller quantized TRT variant (if present), (2) route to Triton shared instance, (3) return 429/503 depending on SLA.
   - Benefit: predictable behavior under OOM storms. Cost: additional routing latency and possible quality degradation. We need automated canaries to verify quality on fallbacks.

Operational notes / debugging:
- Tracing: must propagate request_id across bridge and into CUDA op names; adopt a short binary trace token (16 bytes) that gets attached to stream events for correlation with CPU traces.
- Deterministic reproduction: we build a "replay harness" that replays buffered traces to reproduce memory growth scenarios. This was essential to debug the host-queue accumulation bug.
- Metrics to add: per-engine host-queue-length, async-enqueue-latency, eviction-trigger-count, kvcache-repopulation-rate, per-stream outstanding-allocs.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Kernel preemption limits: which TRT engines can be made preemptible without recompilation? Need a compatibility matrix. (Owner: Jamal)
- Predicted reuse service feasibility: costs of training and drift monitoring vs benefit. Quick A/B recommended. (Owner: Maya)
- Failure modes when Triton backend fails mid-request: should we attempt transparent retry on TRT with partial state? Danger: double-execution. Need safe replay semantics. (Owner: Clara)
- Explore memory-compact KVCache representation (sparse encoding for long contexts) to reduce eviction churn.

Proposed next steps (concrete roadmap):
- Q4 Sprint 1: implement kernel-bridge enqueue API + host-queue metrics + backpressure routing. (2 engineers, 3 weeks)
- Q4 Sprint 2: integrate time-decay KV cache eviction + per-session pinning API + soft quotas. (2 engineers, 3 weeks)
- Q4 Sprint 3: experiment with fallback flows (smaller TRT quantized variant routing and Triton fallback) and run 72-hour soak tests. (2 engineers, 4 weeks)
- Acceptance criteria: end-to-end p99 under mixed traffic within 1.2x Triton baseline while improving throughput by ~10-15% and keeping memory OOM events at zero during 72-hour soak.

Appendix (observed anomalies and notes):
- On H100 we observed lower host enqueue contention than A100 for mixed small-batch workloads; hypothesis: driver/PCIe topology differences and H100's improved async copy throughput.
- CUDA events retention: we found a leak when tracing enabled due to retained event objects in debug builds; added gated tracing to avoid production memory leaks.
- Short note on quantization: INT8 delivered greatest cost savings but required careful calibration; mixed precision fallback should be automated in pipeline to avoid manual operator errors.

Notes-to-self / scratch TODOs:
- Add a simple visualization of queue evolution over 24h to the repo.
- Draft a small runbook for on-call SREs describing fallback signals and mitigations.
- Schedule kernel-interop working session with Triton maintainers to discuss non-preemptive kernels.

References / links:
- internal PRs and replay harness: GH:github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/tree/replay-harness (linked above)
- JIRA: INF-768 covers the kernel-bridge epic

End.
